cards.front: Why does the heart work as a double pump in mammals?
cards.back: The **right side** pumps blood to the lungs and the **left side** pumps it around the body, so blood passes through the heart twice on each complete circuit. This is **double circulation**.
cards.hint: Trace a blood cell from the body back to the body.

cards.front: Why can blood plasma alone not supply enough oxygen to respiring cells?
cards.back: Oxygen dissolves poorly in plasma, so most is carried by **haemoglobin** inside red blood cells. Each haemoglobin binds four oxygen molecules, and the binding is reversible.
cards.hint: Compare how much oxygen plasma holds with what the body needs.

cards.front: Which part of the heart sets the pace of each heartbeat?
cards.back: The **sinoatrial node**, a patch of cells in the right atrium wall, sends out waves of electrical excitation. Heart muscle can contract without nerves starting each beat.
cards.hint: Look for where the electrical wave begins.

cards.front: What is the role of valves in the heart?
cards.back: **Valves** are flaps of tissue that open when the pressure behind them is higher than in front, letting blood flow in one direction only.

cards.front: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right ventricle wall?
cards.back: The left ventricle must create enough pressure to send blood around the whole body, while the right ventricle only serves the nearby lungs.
cards.hint: Compare how far each ventricle sends blood.

cards.front: Why do arteries have elastic fibres in their walls?
cards.back: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at **high pressure**. The elastic fibres stretch as blood surges in and recoil afterwards, which smooths the flow.
cards.hint: Think about the pressure of blood leaving the heart.

cards.front: How is a capillary wall structured to suit exchange?
cards.back: Its wall is **one cell thick**, so substances diffuse across quickly. Dense networks of capillaries give a large surface area for exchange.
cards.hint: Think about the distance substances must travel to reach cells.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say that muscles pull the heart valves open and shut?
cards.back: Valves open and close because of **pressure differences** across them. Muscles do not pull them open or shut.
cards.hint: What actually drives a valve to move?

cards.front: What are the three stages of the cardiac cycle, in order?
cards.back: 1) **Diastole**: the heart relaxes and blood flows into the atria and on into the ventricles. 2) **Atrial systole**: the atria contract and push blood into the ventricles. 3) **Ventricular systole**: the ventricles contract, the atrioventricular valves shut, and the semilunar valves open.
cards.hint: Start with the phase when the heart is filling with blood.

cards.front: What is the role of the atrioventricular node in the heartbeat?
cards.back: It **delays** the wave of excitation briefly before the wave passes to the bottom of the heart and up the ventricle walls.
cards.hint: Think about the order in which the atria and ventricles contract.

cards.front: How is heart rate calculated from the time for one cardiac cycle?
cards.back: Heart rate $= \frac{60\,\mathrm{s}}{t}$, where $t$ is the time for one cycle in seconds. The answer is in $\mathrm{min^{-1}}$, or beats per minute.
cards.hint: Work out how many cycles fit into one minute.

cards.front: A cardiac cycle lasts 0.75 s. What is the heart rate?
cards.back: $\frac{60\,\mathrm{s}}{0.75\,\mathrm{s}} = 80\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$, so the heart rate is 80 beats per minute.
cards.hint: Divide 60 seconds by the length of one cycle.

cards.front: Why does haemoglobin bind oxygen in the lungs but release it in respiring tissues?
cards.back: Haemoglobin binds oxygen where the **partial pressure** of oxygen is high, as in the lungs, and releases it where the partial pressure is low, as in respiring tissues. Partial pressure is measured in kPa.
cards.hint: Compare the oxygen levels in the two places.

cards.back: The **Bohr effect** is the shift of the oxygen dissociation curve to the right when carbon dioxide rises. Haemoglobin then releases more oxygen, which suits active muscles that make more carbon dioxide.
